props.title: Hardcore

sections.content: Hardcore represents Paul Schrader's unflinching dive into America's seedy underbelly, following George C. Scott's devastating performance as a Calvinist father searching for his runaway daughter in the porn industry. The film shares DNA with Taxi Driver (1976), which Schrader wrote, both examining moral crusaders navigating urban decay. Like The Searchers (1956), it's essentially a rescue mission, but Schrader trades Monument Valley for peep shows and adult bookstores, creating a neon-lit nightmare of late 70s exploitation.

sections.content: The film crystallizes key themes that would define Schrader's career - religious faith confronting modern moral decay, sexual taboos, and obsessive male protagonists. These elements surface again in American Gigolo (1980) and Light Sleeper (1992). Scott's Jake VanDorn shares the righteous fury of Death Wish's (1974) Paul Kersey, but Schrader's treatment is more complex, forcing his protagonist to confront his own repression and complicity.

The film's stark portrayal of the adult entertainment industry predates later examinations like Boogie Nights (1997) and 8MM (1999). While those films approached the subject with varying degrees of stylization, Hardcore maintains a documentary-like rawness that makes its descent into darkness all the more affecting. The contrast between Grand Rapids' Calvinist community and Los Angeles' porn underground creates a cultural collision that still resonates. SUBHEAD: Religious Morality Meets Urban Decay

sections.content: Schrader's background in Calvinist Christianity informs every frame, much like his later film First Reformed (2017). The neon-soaked streets of Los Angeles become a modern Sodom, with Scott's VanDorn as an avenging angel who must confront his own rigid worldview. This tension between faith and modernity would become a career-long preoccupation for Schrader, reaching its apex in films like Mishima: A Life in Four Chapters (1985).
